claims.text: Retention of toughness in high-entropy alloys is controlled by suppression of brittle intermetallic precipitation at grain boundaries.
In an as-processed single-phase solid solution, the multi-element configuration inhibits nucleation and growth of embrittling secondary phases.
Extended exposure to elevated temperature can cause diffusion-mediated phase separation.
Elevated-temperature exposure can produce grain-boundary precipitates that act as stress concentrators and reduce toughness.
The proposed initial material is a conventionally processed, homogeneous FCC or BCC single-phase high-entropy alloy without detectable brittle precipitates.
The controlled intervention varies annealing temperature from approximately 600°C to 900°C for one hour, followed by rapid quenching.
Annealing is performed under vacuum or inert gas, and mechanical testing is performed at room temperature.
The structural mediator is the formation of brittle intermetallic precipitates at or near grain boundaries.
Higher annealing temperatures accelerate atomic diffusion sufficiently to overcome barriers to phase separation despite high configurational entropy.
Diffusion-driven phase separation triggers nucleation and growth of secondary intermetallic phases at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary intermetallic phases create stress concentrations and crack-initiation sites.
Formation of grain-boundary intermetallic phases diminishes impact or fracture toughness relative to the as-processed state.
Samples annealed above a critical temperature will have lower Charpy impact energy or fracture toughness than the as-processed baseline.
SEM, TEM, and EDS will reveal increasing amounts of grain-boundary precipitates as annealing temperature increases.
The hypothesis applies to nominally metastable single-phase FCC or BCC high-entropy alloys where diffusion is active but melting or macroscopic phase separation has not occurred.
At extremely high temperatures or in non-metastable compositions, degradation mechanisms other than grain-boundary intermetallic precipitation may dominate.
The onset temperature, precipitation kinetics, and magnitude of toughness loss vary with alloy composition and processing history.

The proposed mechanism is falsified if increasing annealing temperature does not produce both grain-boundary precipitates and a concomitant toughness decrease, or if toughness decreases without brittle precipitate formation.
